parts.note: Jack, as in Jack Tar, is the old nickname for a seaman
to pot is to shoot game, or to shoot a ball into a pocket

explanation.surface: A seaman is told to take a shot at the swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: In cards or gambling, the accumulated stake that a winner takes is called the pool or the big prize.

parts.note: a worn-out nag, a jade, that is also an unlikely shade for a horse

explanation.surface: A veteran horse with an odd coat.
explanation.walkthrough: A jade is an old worn-out horse; a horse coloured green would be unusual indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: The bluish shade of the gemstone nephrite is a recognised colour name.

clue.text: Drink deep from a conveyance on the river

parts.note: a car is a vehicle or conveyance
the Ouse is an English river, the one at York

explanation.surface: Someone drinks heavily aboard a boat on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue CAR sits on top of OUSE, an English river.
explanation.definitionFit: To drink heavily and noisily in company is to booze and make merry.

parts.note: a mail coach rushing with speed, expedition here meaning promptness

explanation.surface: Someone proposes a journey with the postal van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey but means speed; the mail-cart supplies the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with great speed, like a courier, is going with all haste.

clue.text: Brought to heel, they never get drunk

definitions.text: Brought to heel, they never get drunk

parts.words: Brought to heel, they never get drunk
parts.note: metal pieces fixed to shoe heels for dancing, and water outlets that pour drink without drinking

explanation.surface: Disciplined people stay sober.
explanation.walkthrough: Metal plates are fitted to heels of dancing shoes; the faucets dispense drinks but never consume them.
explanation.definitionFit: Faucets pour out drinks for others and plates fitted to shoes are heeled.

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: the girl's letters stand outside, wrapping round the number

parts.note: a girl in a revue who shows everything is a nude
CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A man tries to cuddle one chorus girl picked from a troupe of a hundred and fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace a range of things is to take them in or contain them.

clue.text: The foolishness of getting it teed up in the wrong way

indicators.note: the letters are laid out in a wrong order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A golfer foolishly sets the ball up badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' is a link; 'the wrong way' rearranges IT TEED UP IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineptness or silly clumsiness is a kind of foolishness.

explanation.surface: A dog stands at the top of a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: A pile of stones crowns many a summit, and a small Scottish terrier carries the same name.

explanation.surface: Someone backing military weapons calls it wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: In heraldry, supporters are the beasts holding up a coat of arms; the royal arms have a lion and this one-horned beast. 'Fabulous' means from fable.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-horned beast of myth holds up the Scottish side of the royal coat of arms.

parts.note: the computer that picks the winning premium bond numbers, given a man's name

explanation.surface: A man held as a serf.
explanation.walkthrough: A bondsman is a serf; here it is the British machine named like a man that draws Premium Bond prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment selects the winners among Britain's savings bonds.

indicators.note: the word for skill sits inside the coins' letters

parts.note: a copper is a penny, abbreviated d in old British money, so coppers are ds
art is skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A game of skill played for pennies.
explanation.walkthrough: Before decimalisation a British penny was written d (from Latin denarius); pennies were called coppers.
explanation.definitionFit: The pub contest of throwing small arrows at a board is a well-known game.

clue.text: No price is subject to variation, to be exact

indicators.note: letters liable to vary may be rearranged, so the phrase signals reshuffling

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper explains that prices may change, to be exact about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being exact means acting with accuracy and strict correctness.

clue.text: It's tactless to be left in France

explanation.surface: Someone says it is rude to be abandoned on French soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy and socially awkward behaviour is tactless; the French word for the left-hand side has the same spelling.

parts.note: the light open gig designed for and named after the Hon. Fitzroy ...

explanation.surface: A man named Fitzroy shows off his horse-drawn vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The light one-seat carriage was built in the early 1800s for Fitzroy Stanhope and took his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle named after the man it was built for carries that man's surname.

clue.text: Prepare an old Spaniard for war

parts.note: to arm is to prepare for fighting
aged means old
Don is a Spanish title, so a Spaniard

explanation.surface: Getting an elderly Spanish gentleman ready for battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical final battle at the end of days gives its name to any catastrophic conflict.

parts.note: a bookmaker's price of one to one, and also the numbers that come one above odd ones

explanation.surface: A punter bets a little more than the quoted price.
explanation.walkthrough: In betting the price at which a winning stake is simply doubled is quoted as one to one; numbers one more than odd numbers are the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds of one to one in betting carry this name, and even numbers sit one above odd ones.

parts.note: a reserved, quiet person displays this restraint

explanation.surface: Something is kept on standby to be shown later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' suggests a back-up supply, but here it means the quality of restraint in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Reserve and reluctance to speak freely are the same quality of restraint.

parts.note: not droplets but great falls where a river drops

explanation.surface: A few droplets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' suggests tiny drips; it means places where a river falls steeply.
explanation.definitionFit: Large waterfalls are places where a river plunges.

clue.text: They protect, rather than punish, pupils

definitions.text: They protect, rather than punish, pupils

parts.words: They protect, rather than punish, pupils
parts.note: the pupils are those of the eye, and the strokes of a cane are lashes

explanation.surface: Teachers who shield rather than beat schoolchildren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' are schoolchildren in the surface but parts of the eye; lashes punish schoolboys.
explanation.definitionFit: The hairs fringing the eyelid shield the eye's pupil from dust.

parts.note: the children in her care were little ones, not low fees

explanation.surface: A tradeswoman's fees were modest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like fees, but means the young children someone looks after.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after young children has little ones as her charges.

clue.text: Oils are used to portray her

indicators.note: the paints are worked into a picture, so their letters are rearranged into a new shape

explanation.surface: An artist uses oil paint to paint a woman's portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name stands for the female person the clue calls her.

parts.note: someone minded to join the nobility wants a rank such as lord or earl

explanation.surface: A virtue prized by people of noble character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nobleminded' normally means high-principled; here it means minded to become a noble, who would covet a peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank such as baron or earl is what a would-be aristocrat longs for.

clue.text: After trial, fed with a will

indicators.note: the eating word follows the trial word

parts.note: a test is a trial
ate means fed, took food

explanation.surface: Someone dines heartily after a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With a will' looks like gusto, but means having left a valid will.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who dies leaving a valid legal document disposing of property has died with one.

clue.text: Condescended to take in a shilling as planned

indicators.note: the first word's letters swallow the coin's abbreviation

parts.note: to deign is to condescend to do something
s was the abbreviation for a shilling in old British money

explanation.surface: Someone stooped to accept a shilling, just as was arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: S stood for the shilling, a pre-1971 British coin worth twelve pence.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done by design was intended or arranged beforehand.

explanation.surface: Plants growing at the edge of the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Wharves line a harbour's edge, and the broad-leaved sorrel plants are common weeds.

clue.text: Little, perhaps, but thank heaven for their daily increase

definitions.text: Little, perhaps, but thank heaven for their daily increase

parts.words: Little, perhaps, but thank heaven for their daily increase
parts.note: echoes the song Thank Heaven for Little ... who get bigger every day

explanation.surface: Something small that is still welcome as it grows each day.
explanation.walkthrough: The song from the film Gigi runs 'Thank heaven for little ..., they grow up in the most delightful way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Young females are the subject of Maurice Chevalier's song about little ones growing bigger every day.

indicators.note: the letters are sent running into a new order

explanation.surface: A vehicle is made ready for a drive.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cresta Run at St Moritz is a famous ice track for tobogganing; the toboggan is the car readied for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous ice track at St Moritz bears this name, ridden on toboggans.

clue.text: A time for study in the winter months

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: Winter is the season for books.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or university session is a set period of teaching.

clue.text: Merry monarch has dirge composed by a poet

parts.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme was a merry old soul

indicators.note: the word for a lament is put together afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: A cheerful king has a funeral song written for him by a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merry monarch' suggests Charles II but here is the nursery-rhyme king; 'composed' turns DIRGE into RIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor, author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, was an English Romantic poet.

parts.note: a horse-drawn carriage, and also a private tutor who carries pupils through exams

explanation.surface: A book or lesson that carries knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a large carriage and a private tutor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor who prepares students and a stagecoach share one name.

clue.text: A go-ahead member of the family

definitions.text: A go-ahead member of the family

parts.words: A go-ahead member of the family
parts.note: go ahead suggests step on it, and the relative is a son by remarriage

explanation.surface: An enterprising relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step on it' means go ahead fast; the relative is a boy from a parent's marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A husband's or wife's son from an earlier marriage is a relative by marriage.

clue.text: They must be thoroughly proficient to get past

explanation.surface: Experts insist on high skill from anyone hoping to pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Experts with full command of a craft are its adepts; to overcome or conquer an obstacle is to get past it.
